item.title: xtool-org/xtool
item.description:
Cross-platform Xcode replacement. Build and deploy iOS apps with SwiftPM on Linux, Windows, macOS.

https://xtool.sh

xtool

Cross-platform Xcode replacement. Build and deploy iOS apps with SwiftPM on Linux, Windows, and macOS.

Overview

xtool is a cross-platform (Linux/WSL/macOS) tool that replicates Xcode functionality with open standards.

✅ Build a SwiftPM package into an iOS app

✅ Sign and install iOS apps

✅ Interact with Apple Developer Services programmatically

Getting Started

  1. Follow the guide to install xtool
    • Installation (Linux/Windows)
    • Installation (macOS)
  2. Create and run your first xtool-powered app by following the tutorial!

Examples

Screenshot

Command line interface

$ xtool --help
OVERVIEW: Cross-platform Xcode replacement

USAGE: xtool <subcommand>

OPTIONS:
  -h, --help              Show help information.

CONFIGURATION SUBCOMMANDS:
  setup                   Set up xtool for iOS development
  auth                    Manage Apple Developer Services authentication
  sdk                     Manage the Darwin Swift SDK

DEVELOPMENT SUBCOMMANDS:
  new                     Create a new xtool SwiftPM project
  dev                     Build and run an xtool SwiftPM project
  ds                      Interact with Apple Developer Services

DEVICE SUBCOMMANDS:
  devices                 List devices
  install                 Install an ipa file to your device
  uninstall               Uninstall an installed app
  launch                  Launch an installed app

  See 'xtool help <subcommand>' for detailed help.

Library

You can consume xtool itself as a Swift Package, to enable your own app to interact with Apple Developer Services, iOS devices, and more. You can use this by adding XKit or XToolSupport as a SwiftPM dependency.

Note: while we aim to uphold semver semantics on the CLI interface (breaking change = major version bump), the Swift interface does not offer the same guarantees.

// package dependency:
.package(url: "https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool", .upToNextMinor(from: "1.2.0"))
// target dependency:
.product(name: "XKit", package: "xtool")

item.title: jithin-sabu/purge-app
item.description:
Free up your Mac. Safely. A free, open-source native Mac app that clears the cache and junk your Mac piles up on its own. Files go to the Trash by default, so you can put them back.

https://purgemac.com

Purge

Free up your Mac. Safely.

English | 简体中文 | Русский | Українська

A free, open-source native Mac app that clears the cache and junk your Mac piles up on its own.
Files go to the Trash by default, so you can put them back.

Download  ·  Install guide  ·  Build from source  ·  Security

Your Mac quietly fills up with cache and junk you never see and never asked for. Purge finds it, marks what is safe, and clears it in one click.

Note

Files and folders go to the Trash by default, and Purge never empties the Trash, so you can put them back until you empty it yourself. Deleted permanently: iOS simulators and simulator runtimes, through Xcode's simctl; Xcode's optional Metal Toolchain, through xcodebuild -deleteComponent (Xcode downloads it again when a project needs it); Time Machine local snapshots, through tmutil (Purge keeps the newest and the one from your last backup); the Apple Intelligence models on macOS 27, which Apple's asset service releases and Purge can download again; command-line tools and Homebrew cask apps that their package manager uninstalls, when you choose that in the review sheet. Docker Desktop's folder goes to the Trash. Purge does not run docker system prune.

You do not need to understand any of it to use it. But if you ever want to check, every item carries a plain-language explanation and a safety label, so nothing gets touched that you cannot see and verify first.

Features

Overview

  • Where your space went: one bar for the whole disk. Used, free and total come straight from the volume, so they match System Settings. App Caches, Dev Tools, Large Files, installed apps and leftovers from deleted apps each get their own segment, and the rest is shown as everything else
  • A row per category with its size and share of the disk. Click one to open its tab
  • Everything else opens too. Click the row and a page shows what it holds: four figures for what you can do about the space, over a map where each group is a frame with its biggest folders drawn inside, sized by space and coloured by kind. The kinds are space you free in another app (Photos, Mail, Steam, the Trash), your own files (projects, documents), what Purge leaves alone because it doesn't consider it safe to delete (caches off its list, app data no installed app claims), and what macOS manages. Point at a tile to name it, and click it to see what it is, with Show in Finder or the owning app's own way to free it. It is read only: nothing on it moves a file
  • Scan Everything (⇧⌘R) scans every category, one at a time so the Mac stays responsive. When you open Purge it does the same on its own. Large Files, the app list and leftovers need Full Disk Access. Without it Purge still scans App Caches and Dev Tools, and skips the places macOS protects, such as sandboxed apps' caches
  • Each byte is counted once: an app's cache folder counts under App Caches, not again under the app
  • Hidden in System Data: a card under the categories for space macOS counts as System Data. Its Time Machine snapshots row is where you remove local snapshots, and on macOS 27 it also holds the Apple Intelligence models
  • Apple Intelligence models (macOS 27, Apple silicon): the on-device models macOS files under System Data, with no switch to remove them. Remove releases them through Apple's asset service and installs a profile, which you approve once, so they don't download again. Download Again asks you to remove the profile in System Settings, then asks macOS for the sets Purge removed, in your Siri language. The size shown is Apple's figure; Purge records what the disk really gave back

App Caches

Scans ~/Library/Caches, sandbox container caches (these need Full Disk Access), and common system junk:

  • Per-app cache folders with friendly names, brand icons, and a plain-language explanation if you want to read it
  • System Junk like application logs, crash reports, macOS installers, and leftover macOS update files
  • Large media caches from creative apps like Premiere Pro and After Effects
  • Duplicate cache locations for the same app merged into a single row
  • Results stream in as they are found

Dev Tools

Five groups in one view:

  • Global dev tool caches: Xcode (Derived Data, Archives, DeviceSupport), Homebrew, npm, pnpm, Yarn, CocoaPods, Gradle, the Dart and Flutter pub cache, Docker Desktop, VS Code, Cursor, JetBrains, Cargo, Terraform, and more
  • iOS Simulators: every simulator that is shut down, one row each. A running simulator is listed so its space is counted, but it can't be selected
  • Simulator Runtimes: one row per runtime that simctl reports as deletable
  • Xcode Components: Xcode's optional Metal Toolchain (about 900 MB), removed with xcodebuild -deleteComponent when a full Xcode lists it as installed
  • Developer projects: node_modules, Python virtual environments, Rust target, Flutter build output, Xcode Pods, Android .gradle, and other artifacts grouped by project

Simulators, runtimes and Xcode components are always Check First. They are deleted permanently, not moved to the Trash, and their section headers say so.

In Settings → Cleaning, choose Projects count as stale after (1 month to 2 years, or Show all) to control which projects appear. Age is measured from the last time anything in the project changed, including git activity, not from the date on node_modules or target. A project in use right now, with a terminal or dev server running inside it or a git command in progress, never appears.

Git worktrees made by AI coding tools (Cursor, Codex, Conductor, T3 Code, and Claude Code) appear under Orphaned Git Worktrees only once their repository no longer lists them. A worktree Git still uses never appears however old it is, and neither does one a terminal or agent is working inside.

Large Files

Find space-hogging personal files without digging through folders:

  • Scans Documents, Desktop, Downloads, Movies, Music, and Pictures, plus ~/Parallels and ~/Virtual Machines.localized for virtual machines only, and iCloud Drive's own folder for files you can keep only in iCloud
  • A folder you moved and replaced with a link, such as ~/Documents pointing to another drive, is scanned where the link leads when that is inside your home folder or on a drive under /Volumes, on a disk attached to your Mac. Its files are listed by their real path and go to that drive's Trash. A link anywhere else, such as into ~/Library/CloudStorage, to a network share, or to a whole drive or a copy of a Mac, is not followed, and the scan says where it leads. Links inside the folders are never followed
  • Skips managed libraries (Photos, iMovie, Music, and similar), hidden folders, and project folders like node_modules, Pods, DerivedData and build output. Deleting a single file out of a dependency tree only breaks the install, so those belong in Dev Tools, which removes them a folder at a time
  • Search filters the list as you type, matching the file name, the folder it sits in, and its source label
  • Filter by size (5 MB to 1 GB) and last used (any time up to over 1 year ago)
  • Category chips for videos, audio, images, PDFs, archives, documents, AI models, virtual machines, and other files
  • Duplicates: a byte-for-byte scan finds identical copies, groups them together, and shows how much you'd reclaim by keeping one. A Duplicates chip gathers them in one place. Delete extra copies clears a whole tab of duplicates in one go. It suggests a copy to keep per set and marks the rest for Trash, and you can move the keeper to a different copy before anything is deleted. Nothing is removed until you review and confirm
  • Sort by size, date, or name; select files and review before deleting
  • Quick Look preview and Show in Finder from each row
  • Deletions move files to Trash, so nothing is permanently erased
  • Keep Only in iCloud frees the space an iCloud file takes on this Mac and keeps the file in iCloud, the same as Finder's Remove Download. The iCloud chip lists the synced files that also use space here, with how much you'd free, and the action sits there and in each synced file's right-click menu. The file stays in its folder in Finder with a cloud mark, and opening it downloads it again. Purge offers it only for files fully uploaded to iCloud, with no sync conflict, not set to Keep Downloaded, not hard-linked and unchanged for five minutes. It checks all of that again just before it acts on each file, and skips any file that is open in an app. Files in iCloud Drive's own folder are never offered for the Trash, since trashing them removes them from your other devices. It is never part of Clean Safe Items or a scheduled clean

Large Files is separate from cache cleanup: these are your personal files, not rebuildable caches.

Restore images, virtual machines, and unfinished downloads

Some big files carry a label that says what they are. Hover it for the full explanation.

  • Restore image: a macOS .ipsw, often 15 to 25 GB. It's only needed to set up a Mac, a device, or a virtual machine.
  • Virtual machine: a Parallels (.pvm), UTM (.utm), or VMware Fusion (.vmwarevm) bundle. It's one row and goes to the Trash whole, never a disk file from inside it. If the app is still installed, the label says to remove the VM there, since the app keeps its own list. A VM whose app is open, or that holds a lock file, stays off the list until you quit the app.
  • Unfinished download: .crdownload, .part, and Parallels' .prlupd-part files, and Safari's .download bundle when it sits directly in Downloads.

Local AI models

Downloaded models are often the largest files on a Mac and are easy to forget. They appear in Large Files under the AI Models category, one row per model, named the way you installed it, with the app or library that downloaded it as the location. Purge knows the stores of Ollama, LM Studio, the Hugging Face Hub cache (~/.cache/huggingface/hub; HF_HOME and HF_HUB_CACHE are honoured when they are set for apps, not only in a shell profile), swift-transformers, apps that keep models under ~/Library/Caches/huggingface, PyTorch Hub, Whisper, GPT4All, Jan, DiffusionBee and Draw Things. Weight files over 100 MB in ~/Library/Caches, ~/Library/Application Support and ~/.cache that belong to no known store are listed too, by the folder they sit in, so you can tell which app downloaded them.

Purge understands Ollama's content-addressed storage, so a model's size counts only the bytes that would actually be reclaimed rather than blobs shared with another model. A Hugging Face model is its whole cache folder, so a blob two snapshots share is counted once and never removed from under the other. Models always go to the Trash and are never part of Clean Safe Items or a scheduled clean. When an app keeps its own list of installed models that Purge can't update, the row says the app may still show the model as installed.

App Uninstaller

Dragging an app to the Trash leaves most of it behind: caches, preferences, containers, saved state, logs, cookies and website data, and login helpers pile up on disk. The Uninstaller removes the app and those leftovers in one pass.

  • Lists the apps you installed in Applications and ~/Applications, in the Applications folder at the top of any drive you plug in, and in folders you add under Settings > Where Purge looks for apps (or from the hint under the app list), skipping system apps and Purge itself. Each tile shows what an uninstall would free: the app bundle plus the leftovers Purge matched to it
  • Apps from one vendor that share a folder, such as the four apps in /Applications/DaVinci Resolve, show as one entry that opens to its apps
  • Select one or more apps, then review a sheet with a section per app that lists every item with its path and size
  • Matching is strict, so uninstalling one app can't sweep in files shared across a vendor's apps. Every match arrives checked, and you untick what you want to keep. Three kinds start unticked: a hidden folder in your home folder that holds the app's settings, an Application Scripts folder with scripts in it, and anything another installed app still uses, which is held back and marked "Kept, still used by" that app
  • A running app is asked to quit first, and only gracefully. If it won't, it's left installed and the rest of the batch still goes through
  • Everything confirmed moves to Trash through the same delete engine as the rest of Purge, so it can all come back. The one exception is an app Homebrew installed as a cask: the review sheet offers two buttons, Remove with Homebrew and Move All to Trash, and says that Homebrew deletes the app permanently and runs the cask's own uninstall steps, which can stop its background services and delete its helper tools and installer files permanently too. A cask that installs several apps is never offered to Homebrew. Its leftovers still go to the Trash, and if Homebrew refuses, the app goes to the Trash instead
  • Optional, off by default: turn on Review leftovers when an app is deleted in Settings. A small background watcher then notices when an app leaves one of those folders — even if Purge is quit — opens Purge with just that app's leftovers, and gets out of the way after you confirm or dismiss. Nothing moves without that review. In this review only exact bundle-id and app-group matches inside your home folder arrive checked; looser name-only matches arrive unchecked for you to confirm
  • Some apps are installed under an administrator, so your account can't move them to the Trash, and the same goes for their leftovers in /Library. Turn on Remove admin-locked apps without a password in Settings and a small helper that runs as root moves them to your Trash. It moves only paths the uninstaller approved, and leftover macOS update files. On a standard account the setting reads Remove admin-locked apps, and Purge asks for an administrator's name and password each time
  • You can start from Finder too: turn on Uninstall from Finder's right-click menu in Settings, then right-click an app and choose Uninstall with Purge. Dropping an app on Purge's Dock icon does the same

The Uninstaller has two more lists beside Installed Apps. Each appears when its scan finds something:

  • Leftovers: files left behind by apps that are already gone, grouped by how Purge matched them to the app. Nothing is selected for you
  • Command-Line Tools: tools installed by a script go to the Trash: the tool's folder in your home folder, the commands in ~/.local/bin that start it, and its background jobs. Tools installed by Homebrew, npm, pipx, uv or Cargo are removed by that manager's own uninstall, permanently. The confirmation lists the two groups separately

Safety labels

Purge assigns a safety label to every item it recognizes:

Label Meaning
✅ Safe to Clean Known cache or rebuildable artifact, safe to remove
⚠️ Check First May be safe, but could cause inconvenience

Filter with All, Safe to Clean, or Check First (⌥⌘1–⌥⌘3). Sort by size, date modified, or name.

Unidentified folders are left out of the list entirely. Purge only shows what it knows about.

The labels and explanations are there to be checked, not read cover to cover. Select the safe items and clean them, or open the reasoning behind any single row first. Either way is fine.

Cleaning

  • Clean Selected: pick specific rows, review in a confirmation sheet, then delete. Git and lockfile checks run before anything is removed
  • Clean Safe Items: on the Overview, moves every Safe to Clean item to the Trash after one confirmation
  • Clean Safe Files: the same safe cleanup from the menu bar
  • Scheduled cleaning: in Settings → Cleaning, turn on Clean automatically and choose how often (weekly, monthly, every 3 months, or a Custom interval you set in days, weeks, or months). Purge sends a local reminder when a clean is due and runs it the next time you open or switch to Purge, so the cleanup keeps happening without you thinking about it. It never cleans in the background
  • Files and folders move to the Trash. Purge never empties the Trash. iOS simulators and simulator runtimes are deleted permanently through Xcode's simctl. The Metal Toolchain is deleted permanently through xcodebuild -deleteComponent, and Xcode downloads it again when a project needs it. Time Machine local snapshots are deleted permanently through tmutil; Purge keeps the newest and the one from your last backup. The Apple Intelligence models are released through Apple's asset service and can be downloaded again. Tools and cask apps a package manager installed are removed by that manager's own uninstall, permanently, when you pick that in the review sheet

Settings

Settings is a tab in the sidebar (⌘,) with five groups:

  • General: Keep Purge in the menu bar, which is off on a new install. When it is on, Purge keeps running after you close the window, and you can also choose Launch Purge at login and Hide Dock icon. Appearance is Auto, Light, or Dark
  • Cleaning: Clean automatically, with a frequency and the next-clean date. Projects count as stale after, the threshold for Developer Projects. Excluded folders, the folders you've told Purge to leave alone, each with its current size. Right-click a row in App Caches, Dev Tools or Large Files and choose Exclude from scans to add one. An excluded simulator runtime is listed by name and build, with the size it had when you excluded it. Excluding only ever narrows what Purge looks at
  • Uninstalling: Uninstall from Finder's right-click menu, Where Purge looks for apps, Review leftovers when an app is deleted, and Remove admin-locked apps without a password
  • Updates and History: Check for updates automatically, Install updates automatically, and Cleaning history, which lists every automatic and manual clean with the space freed and the item count, and shows a summary of the last one. Open a clean to see what was moved to the Trash, what was deleted permanently, and what was skipped
  • Uninstall: Uninstall Purge, covered under Uninstalling

More

  • First-run onboarding: a welcome, a first scan, and the results with a button that moves the safe items to the Trash. Last comes an optional request for Full Disk Access, shown only if Purge doesn't have it
  • Menu bar companion: recoverable space at a glance, quick open, and scan/clean actions. It is optional and off on a new install; turn on Keep Purge in the menu bar in Settings
  • Shortcuts and Spotlight: three actions, Scan for Junk, Clean Safe Junk, and Uninstall an App
  • Languages: the app is in English, Simplified Chinese, Russian and Turkish, and follows your system language
  • Disk summary: the Overview shows used and free space; the sidebar shows what is already in the Trash, and each scan tab's size
  • In-app updates: the About screen checks for, downloads, and installs new versions

Keyboard shortcuts

Shortcut Action
⌘R Scan the current tab (Scan Everything on the Overview)
⇧⌘R Scan Everything, from any tab
⌘1–⌘5 Go to Overview, App Caches, Dev Tools, Large Files, or App Uninstaller
⌥⌘1–⌥⌘3 Filter by All, Safe to Clean, or Check First, on App Caches and Dev Tools
⌘F Search on Large Files and App Uninstaller
⌘, Open Settings

Download

Installation

There are two ways to install Purge: with Homebrew if you live in the terminal, or by downloading the app directly. Both land in the same place.

Install with Homebrew

brew install --cask purge

This installs Purge from the official Homebrew cask, and Homebrew verifies the download's checksum for you automatically.

Install manually

The steps below walk through the direct download.

Step 1: Download

Click the download link above and download the .dmg.

Step 2: Verify your download (optional but recommended)

Tip

Since Purge deletes files, verifying the checksum confirms your download is byte-for-byte the one that was published, with nothing altered in transit.

Each release includes a matching .dmg.sha256 checksum file. Download both the .dmg and its .dmg.sha256 file into the same folder, then in Terminal:

cd ~/Downloads
shasum -a 256 -c Purgev*.dmg.sha256

A result ending in OK means the file matches the published release.

Step 3: Install

Open the .dmg and drag Purge to your Applications folder.

Step 4: Open Purge

Double-click Purge to open it. Purge is notarized by Apple, so it opens normally with no extra steps.

Step 5: Let Purge look deeper (optional)

Purge works without Full Disk Access: it scans App Caches and Dev Tools. With it, Purge also finds App Store apps' caches, large files, installed apps and deleted apps' leftovers.

  1. At the end of the first run, or later from Look deeper, click Let Purge in. System Settings opens
  2. Find Purge in the list and turn on its switch
  3. Come back to Purge. It notices the change by itself. If macOS offers to reopen Purge, go ahead

Choose Not now to skip it. You can turn the access off anytime in System Settings.

Updating

Purge updates itself in place. Once a day it checks for a new version, and when one is available the update window appears with the release notes. Choose Install Update and Purge downloads it, verifies its signature, installs it, and relaunches. You don't need to visit the release page or drag anything.

By default nothing is installed without your confirmation. You can also check whenever you like from the About screen, and if you'd rather Purge didn't check on its own, turn off Check for updates automatically in Settings → Updates and History.

If you'd rather not be asked, turn on Install updates automatically in the same place, or tick the matching box in the update window. New versions then download in the background and install the next time Purge quits. Once one is ready, Restart to Update in the Purge menu, the menu bar menu or the About screen installs it straight away. That helps if you keep Purge in the menu bar and rarely quit it.

Updates are delivered through Sparkle, the standard update framework for Mac apps outside the App Store. Each update is signed with a key that lives only on the developer's machine, and Purge refuses any download that doesn't carry a matching signature.

Updating with Homebrew

If you installed through Homebrew, you can update from the terminal instead:

brew upgrade --cask purge

Either route is fine. Your settings, cleaning schedule, and history are kept whichever way you update; they live separately from the app. You won't need to grant Full Disk Access again either, since the permission stays with Purge.

You can also browse past versions on the releases page anytime.

Uninstalling

Choose Uninstall Purge… in the Purge menu, or Settings → Uninstall → Uninstall…. Purge lists what it runs in the background on your Mac (the deleted-app watcher, the admin helper, the Finder right-click item, the cleanup reminder and launch at login), turns each one off and checks it really stopped, then moves itself to the Trash and quits.

Your settings and cleaning history stay on your Mac, so a reinstall picks up where you left off. Tick Also move settings and history to the Trash to move them too. Nothing is deleted permanently; you empty the Trash when you're ready.

macOS doesn't let an app remove its own Full Disk Access. If Purge had it, the last screen offers Quit and Open Full Disk Access. In System Settings, select Purge and click the minus button.

Already dragged Purge to the Trash? Download it again, open it, and choose Uninstall Purge…, so nothing it ran keeps running. To check nothing is left, Purge should be gone from System Settings → General → Login Items & Extensions, and this should print nothing:

pgrep -fl io.getpurge

Build from source

Prefer to build Purge yourself instead of downloading the release? Here is how.

Prerequisites

  • macOS 13.0 or later
  • Xcode 26 or later (from the Mac App Store). The project uses Swift 6.2 build settings (default actor isolation and approachable concurrency) and @concurrent, which need Xcode 26; earlier versions won't build it
  • Node.js 18+ and npm, only needed if you want to regenerate brand icons

Dependencies are resolved by Swift Package Manager when you first build. The only one is Sparkle, which handles in-app updates.

Step 1: Clone the repo

git clone https://github.com/jithin-sabu/purge-app.git
cd purge-app

Step 2: Build and run

Open the project in Xcode and run:

open purge.xcodeproj

Then select the purge scheme and press ⌘R.

The project is set to sign with the developer's Developer ID certificate, which you won't have. In Xcode, open Signing & Capabilities for each target and choose your own team or Sign to Run Locally.

Or build straight from the command line, with signing turned off:

# Build a Debug app
xcodebuild -project purge.xcodeproj -scheme purge -configuration Debug build CODE_SIGN_IDENTITY="" CODE_SIGNING_REQUIRED=NO CODE_SIGNING_ALLOWED=NO

# Build a Release app
xcodebuild -project purge.xcodeproj -scheme purge -configuration Release build CODE_SIGN_IDENTITY="" CODE_SIGNING_REQUIRED=NO CODE_SIGNING_ALLOWED=NO

The built Purge.app is written under Xcode's DerivedData folder (the build output ends with its path). macOS treats each build without your signature as a new app, so Full Disk Access has to be granted again after a rebuild.

Optional: regenerate brand icons

The app cache icons are generated from simple-icons. To rebuild them:

npm install
npm run generate:icons

Running the tests

xcodebuild test -project purge.xcodeproj -scheme purge -destination 'platform=macOS' CODE_SIGN_IDENTITY="" CODE_SIGNING_REQUIRED=NO CODE_SIGNING_ALLOWED=NO

The signing flags matter: without a development certificate on the machine, the test build fails before a single test runs. Continuous integration builds the same way.

Requirements

  • macOS 13.0 or later
  • Full Disk Access (optional; Large Files, the App Uninstaller and leftovers need it)
  • Xcode (optional, for iOS simulators and simulator runtimes). If you deleted Xcode, Purge still finds the simulators it left behind

Privacy

Purge runs entirely on your Mac. Your excluded folders, cleaning history and last scan stay in its Application Support folder, and your settings in its preferences. Nothing is uploaded. The last scan is saved so Purge has something to show while it scans again. Nothing from Desktop, Documents, Downloads or iCloud is written to it, and Large Files keeps only its totals, by kind of file, never a file name.

The one time Purge talks to the network is the update check: once a day it fetches a small XML file from GitHub to see whether a newer version is available. It sends nothing about you or your Mac, and you can turn it off in Settings → Updates and History.

Purge reads some file contents, on your Mac only. To find duplicates it compares files of the same size byte for byte. To work out which app or tool a file belongs to, it reads small files such as an app's Info.plist, LaunchAgent plists, and the scripts that start command-line tools. It never sends file contents anywhere.

Purge does not use AI. Nothing you scan or clean is sent to an AI service.

Security

Purge deletes files, so safety is the point. A few things worth knowing:

  • Trash by default: Files and folders move to the macOS Trash, and Purge never empties it. You can restore them until you empty the Trash yourself. iOS simulators and simulator runtimes are deleted permanently through simctl. Xcode's Metal Toolchain is deleted permanently through xcodebuild -deleteComponent and downloads again when a project needs it. Time Machine local snapshots are deleted permanently through tmutil; Purge keeps the newest and the one from your last backup. The Apple Intelligence models are released through Apple's asset service and can be downloaded again from Purge. Command-line tools and Homebrew cask apps you choose to remove through their package manager are deleted by that manager, permanently. Docker Desktop's data folder goes to the Trash. Purge does not run docker system prune.
  • Allowlist-based deletion: Only paths that match an explicit safety allowlist are ever eligible for cleanup. Anything Purge does not recognize is never touched. The safety page lists every allowed location and everything Purge will never touch, generated from the app's source.
  • You choose what goes: Purge shows what is reclaimable and you decide what to clear.
  • Root helper, off by default: To move apps an administrator installed, Purge can install a small helper that runs as root. It stays off until you turn on Remove admin-locked apps without a password and approve it in System Settings. It does one thing: it moves a path the uninstaller approved, or a leftover macOS update file, to your Trash. Its source is in PurgeHelper/.
  • Open source: The full deletion logic, including the allowlist, is in this repo for you to read or build from source yourself.
  • Notarized by Apple: The app is signed and notarized, so macOS can verify it hasn't been tampered with since release.
  • Signed updates: In-app updates are verified against a signing key before they are installed. An update that isn't signed by that key is refused, so a compromised download can't become a compromised install.

Found a safety gap or a path that could be deleted when it shouldn't be? Please report it. See SECURITY.md for how.

Contributing

Bug reports, safety findings, and pull requests are welcome. CONTRIBUTING.md covers how to set up the project and what makes a change easy to review. Anything touching the safety allowlist, the never-delete protections, or the scanning logic gets extra scrutiny and takes longer to review, which is deliberate.

Security issues are the exception: report those privately through SECURITY.md rather than opening an issue.

item.title: LiveContainer/LiveContainer
item.description:
Run iOS apps without actually installing them!

LiveContainer

An app launcher that runs iOS apps without actually installing them!

Crowdin Project:  |   Documentation:livecontainer.github.io

LiveContainer

  • LiveContainer is an app launcher (not emulator or hypervisor) that allows you to run iOS apps inside it.
  • Allows you to install unlimited apps (3 app/10 app id free developer account limit does not apply here) with only one app & app id. You can also have multiple versions of an app installed with multiple data containers.
  • (Below iOS 26) When JIT is available, codesign is entirely bypassed, no need to sign your apps before installing. Otherwise, your app will be signed with the same certificate used by LiveContainer.

Caution

Important Notice Regarding Third-Party Builds of LiveContainer

We have recently noticed the appearance of certain closed-source third-party builds of LiveContainer. Please be aware that all your apps are installed within LiveContainer, which means these third-party builds have full access to your data, including sensitive information such as keychain items and login credentials.

Furthermore, please note that we do not provide any support for issues of these third-party builds.

Installation

LiveContainer comes with a standalone version and a version with built-in SideStore. Please read the install guide here

If you encounter any issue please read our FAQ here

Standalone

Stable
Nightly

LiveContainer+SideStore

Stable Nightly

Requirements

  • iOS/iPadOS 15+
    • Multitasking requires iOS/iPadOS 16.0+
  • AltStore 2.0+ / SideStore 0.6.0+

Features & Guides

Installing Apps

  • Open LiveContainer, tap the plus icon in the upper right hand corner and select IPA files to install.
  • Choose the app you want to open in the next launch.
  • You can long-press the app to manage it.

Add Apps to Home Screen

Multiple LiveContainers

Using multiple LiveContainers allows you to run multiples different apps simultaneously, with almost seamless data transfer between the LiveContainers.

Multitasking

You can now launch multiple apps simultaneously in in-app virtual windows. These windows can be resized, scaled, and even displayed using the native Picture-in-Picture (PiP) feature. On iPads, apps can run in native window mode, displaying each app in a separate system window. And if you wish, you can choose to run apps in multitasking mode by default in settings.

To use multitasking, hold its banner and tap "Multitask". You can also make Multitask the default launch mode in settings.

Note

  1. To use multitasking, ensure you select "Keep App Extensions" when installing via SideStore/AltStore.
  2. If you want to enable JIT for multitasked apps, you’ll need a JIT enabler that supports attaching by PID. (StikDebug)

JIT Support

Installing external tweaks

Multiple Containers/External Containers

Hiding Apps

Fix File Picker & Local Notification

Some apps may experience issues with their file pickers or not be able to apply for notification permission in LiveContainer. To resolve this, enable "Fix File Picker" & "Fix Local Notifications" accordingly in the app-specific settings.

"Open In App" Support

  • You can simply share a URL or a file to app simply by using iOS's native share sheet. In share sheet, select LiveContainer, and LiveContainer will ask you which app you'd like to open that URL/file in.
  • What's more, you also can tap the link icon in the top-right corner of the "Apps" tab and input the URL. LiveContainer will detect the appropriate app and ask if you want to launch it.

Compatibility

Unfortunately, not all apps work in LiveContainer, so we have a compatibility list to tell if there is apps that have issues. If they aren't on this list, then it's likely going run. However, if it doesn't work, please make an issue about it.

Building

Open Xcode, edit DEVELOPMENT_TEAM[config=Debug] in xcconfigs/Global.xcconfig to your team id and compile.

Project structure

Main executable

  • Core of LiveContainer
  • Contains the logic of setting up guest environment and loading guest app.
  • If no app is selected, it loads LiveContainerSwiftUI.

LiveContainerSwiftUI

  • SwiftUI rewrite of LiveContainerUI (by @hugeBlack)
  • Language file Localizable.xcstrings is in here for multilingual support. To help us translate LiveContainer, please visit our crowdin project

MultitaskSupport

  • Contains the implementation of multitasking feature.
  • Based on FrontBoardAppLauncher

SideStore

  • Supporting code for SideStore's app refreshing integration

TweakLoader

  • A simple tweak injector, which loads CydiaSubstrate and loads tweaks.
  • Injected to every app you install in LiveContainer.

ZSign

  • The app signer shipped with LiveContainer.
  • Originally made by zhlynn.
  • LiveContainer uses Feather's version of ZSign modified by khcrysalis.
  • Changes are made to meet LiveContainer's needs.

How does it work?

Patching guest executable

  • Patch __PAGEZERO segment:
    • Change vmaddr to 0xFFFFC000 (0x100000000 - 0x4000)
    • Change vmsize to 0x4000
  • Change MH_EXECUTE to MH_DYLIB.
  • Inject a load command to load TweakLoader.dylib

Patching @executable_path

  • Hook dyld4::APIs::_NSGetExecutablePath
  • Call _NSGetExecutablePath
  • Replace config.process.mainExecutablePath
    • Calculate address of config.process.mainExecutablePath using dyld4::APIs instance (passed as first parameter)
    • Use builtin_vm_protect or TPRO unlock to make it writable
    • Replace the address with one we have control of
  • Put the original dyld4::APIs::_NSGetExecutablePath back

Old Method

  • Call _NSGetExecutablePath with an invalid buffer pointer input -> SIGSEGV
  • Do some magic stuff to overwrite the contents of executable_path.

Patching NSBundle.mainBundle

  • This property is overwritten with the guest app's bundle.

Bypassing Library Validation

  • JIT is optional to bypass codesigning. In JIT-less mode, all executables are signed so this does not apply.
  • Derived from Restoring Dyld Memory Loading

dlopening the executable

  • Call dlopen with the guest app's executable
  • TweakLoader loads all tweaks in the selected folder
  • Find the entry point
  • Jump to the entry point
  • The guest app's entry point calls UIApplicationMain and start up like any other iOS apps.

Multi-Account support & Keychain Semi-Separation

128 keychain access groups are created and LiveContainer allocates them randomly to each container of the same app. So you can create 128 container with different keychain access groups.

Limitations

  • Entitlements from the guest app are not applied to the host app. This isn't a big deal since sideloaded apps requires only basic entitlements.
  • App Permissions are globally applied.
  • Guest app containers are not sandboxed. This means one guest app can access other guest apps' data.
  • App extensions aren't supported. they cannot be registered because: LiveContainer is sandboxed, SpringBoard doesn't know what apps are installed in LiveContainer, and they take up App ID.
  • Multitasking can be achieved by using multiple LiveContainer and the multitasking feature. However, while we were able to fix physical keyboard input issue on iPadOS (https://github.com/LiveContainer/LiveContainer/issues/524), iPhone Mirroring uses different checks which still broke it (https://github.com/LiveContainer/LiveContainer/issues/793).
  • Remote push notification will not work
  • Querying custom URL schemes might not work(?)

TODO

  • Use ChOma instead of custom MachO parser

License

  • LinusHenze's CFastFind: MIT license
  • litehook: MIT license

  • @Vishram1123 for the initial shortcut implementation.
  • @hugeBlack for SwiftUI contribution
  • @Staubgeborener for automatic AltStore/SideStore source updater
  • @fkunn1326 for improved app hiding
  • @slds1 for dynamic color feature
  • @Vishram1123 for iOS 26+ JIT Script Support

item.title: lingyired/status-trio
item.description:
Status Trio — a native macOS app that combines Wi-Fi, battery, and volume into one compact, configurable status icon for the menu bar, the Dock, or both, inspired by the iPhone Duo combined status bar.

https://statustrio.lingai.net/

Status Trio

Three system signals. One native macOS status icon — in your menu bar or the Dock.

Want to see it in action first? Open statustrio.lingai.net to simulate every icon state in your browser.

English · 简体中文 · 繁體中文 · 日本語 · 한국어 · Español · Français · Deutsch · Português (Brasil) · Русский

Status Trio is a native macOS status app that combines Wi-Fi, battery, and volume into one compact, configurable icon, shown in the menu bar, in the Dock, or in both. Its popover goes deeper than the icon: a Wi-Fi panel for nearby networks and link details, a Bluetooth panel for paired devices, a Battery Details page, and the audio devices that are playing. It is inspired by the iPhone Duo's combined status bar icon for Wi-Fi, Battery, and Cellular Data, adapted for Mac with Volume instead of Cellular Data.

Status Trio is an independent project and is not affiliated with Apple.

Highlights

  • One icon, three signals — battery, Wi-Fi, and volume share one icon in the menu bar, the Dock, or both, and a Bluetooth device that is playing can take the middle spot with its own symbol.
  • Bluetooth — the volume indicator turns blue while it plays. The panel lists paired devices you can tap to connect or disconnect, shows battery levels by default, and stays off until you enable it.
  • Battery — percentage, charging or plugged in, time to full, and a color when it runs low. Open the row for adapter power, voltage, current, cycle count, and Low Power Mode, plus optional estimated power flow and a CPU energy-impact list. Supported Apple silicon Macs on macOS 26.4 or later can also override the charge limit with Charge to Full Now.
  • Wi-Fi — the network you are on and how strong the signal is. Open it to see nearby networks, check the link details, or switch Wi-Fi off. Switching between networks happens in the Wi-Fi pane of System Settings.
  • Volume — level, mute, and the output device, drawn as dots or an arc. Scroll the whole panel or just the control, and pick which direction turns it up.
  • Make it yours — icon size, symbol scale, ring thickness, status colors, and which sections the popover shows, in the order you want.
  • Menu bar, Dock, or both — and the Dock icon can follow the system style or stay dark or light.
  • Native on macOS — left-click opens the popover, right-click opens the menu, and a first-launch guide explains each part of the icon. Ethernet, a hotspot, or Internet Sharing can keep the Wi-Fi glyph if you prefer.
  • Stays current — status comes from system events with a slow poll as a fallback, and Sparkle updates the app through a signed feed.
  • Also included — twelve languages, and an optional launch at login.

Install

Install from the official Homebrew Cask:

brew install --cask status-trio

To update an existing Homebrew installation:

brew upgrade --cask status-trio

Or download the latest StatusTrio-*.dmg from GitHub Releases, open it, and drag Status Trio.app into /Applications.

The official release is signed with Developer ID and notarized by Apple. Open it normally after installation; no quarantine-removal command is needed. In-app updates use Sparkle with EdDSA signature verification.

Input, audio, and everyday controls

  • Input-source icon — show the current input method in the middle of the menu bar and Dock icon instead of the network glyph. Choose Current Input Source under Settings › App Icon › Middle Icon; choose an enabled input source from the panel to switch to it.
  • Global shortcut — assign a shortcut in Settings › General to open or close the status panel from another app. No shortcut is assigned by default.
  • Bluetooth controls — turn Bluetooth on or off from the panel, connect or disconnect paired devices, and switch listening modes on supported AirPods and HUAWEI FreeBuds. Optional Apple-device battery rows are configured in Settings › Bluetooth; availability depends on the device and connection.
  • Audio input and output — select speakers or microphones, adjust output and input levels, and control compatible external-display speakers through DDC. Display volume support depends on the hardware and connection.
  • Charging and appearance — enable charging effects for the menu bar and Dock. On macOS 26 and later, the app icon in Finder and Launchpad also follows the system light or dark appearance.

Bluetooth audio

Pick Bluetooth Device as the middle icon under Settings › App Icon › Middle Icon and the middle glyph becomes that device's own symbol while it plays — AirPods, headphones, speakers, and other devices supply their own — and the volume dots or arc can turn blue. Show network problems instead, on by default, keeps the network icon while the connection itself is in trouble. The same picker also offers Network, Current Input Source, Battery Percentage, and Power (Watts):

The popover's Bluetooth row reports live state: the names of connected devices and, for AirPods, left, right, and case battery. The Bluetooth panel lists paired devices and their connection state: tap a device to connect it, tap a connected one to disconnect — keyboards, mice, trackpads and gamepads ask for confirmation in the row first. The panel is off by default, is enabled under Settings › Status Panel, and asks for Bluetooth permission on first use. Settings › Bluetooth also controls whether the battery levels are read — on by default — lists the paired devices so you can drag them into the order the panel shows and set how many appear, and scales the Bluetooth icon from 100% to 180%.

Dock icon

The same live icon can live in the Dock instead of the menu bar, or in both places at once:


Dock icon in dark appearance


Dock icon in light appearance


Bluetooth panel preview

The Dock icon draws the same combined icon as the menu bar, so with Bluetooth Device selected as the middle icon the device glyph takes over the middle there too. Its background can follow the system icon style or be pinned to a fixed shade:

Icon states

Every state the combined icon can show, drawn by the app's own renderer — battery indicators on top, Wi-Fi (or the Bluetooth audio device that can replace it, when that option is on) in the middle, and volume dots or the arc at the bottom, turning blue while a Bluetooth device is playing:

The same states rendered for a dark menu bar:

Requirements

  • macOS 13 deployment target; Ventura runtime validation pending
  • Swift 6 toolchain with the macOS 26 SDK or newer to build it; the formal release workflow uses the xcode-27 runner and Xcode 27. Building against an older SDK silently produces the pre-Tahoe popover appearance, so scripts/build-app.sh fails when the SDK is older than 26.

Run from source

git clone https://github.com/lingyired/status-trio.git
cd status-trio
swift run StatusTrio

Build a local app

Build an ad-hoc-signed app bundle and launch it:

bash scripts/build-app.sh release

The bundle is created at dist/StatusTrio.app. To build without quitting or launching an existing instance, run:

bash scripts/build-app.sh release no-open

The ad-hoc-signed bundle is intended for local personal use. Gatekeeper may reject it if the bundle is transferred with quarantine metadata.

Usage

  • Left-click the menu bar icon or the Dock icon to open the status popover.
  • Right-click either icon for the native menu, including version and quit actions.
  • Select the Wi-Fi or battery row in the popover to open its page: nearby networks and link details, or Battery Details. The Bluetooth row lists its paired devices in place — tap one to connect or disconnect — with an Expand control when they do not all fit.
  • Open Settings to choose where the icon is shown (menu bar, Dock, or both) and to change its size, colors, ring thickness, the panel sections and their order, scroll-to-adjust behavior, language, update checks, and launch at login.
  • Reopen the Meet your icon guide any time from Settings › App Icon › Open Guide.
  • Enable the current Wi-Fi network name when prompted; macOS requests location access for this optional detail.

Known limitations

Two boundaries macOS and this project draw deliberately. Both are explained in Known limitations.

  • Switching networks happens in System Settings. Choosing a network in the popover opens the Wi-Fi pane; Status Trio never reads or stores Wi-Fi passwords, because macOS offers no public API to connect with a saved password and every alternative ends with the app holding them.
  • Charge-limit control uses a private interface. The opt-in Charge to Full Now action appears only on supported Apple silicon Macs on macOS 26.4 or later, uses a private PowerUI interface, and can be turned off in Battery settings; availability and behavior depend on macOS. The limit may stay at 100% after charging or unplugging and is not restored automatically, so restore it in System Settings if needed. Low Power Mode uses a separate opt-in privileged helper.

Languages

Status Trio follows the macOS preferred language by default and includes English, Simplified Chinese, Traditional Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Spanish, French, German, Italian, Brazilian Portuguese, Russian, and Arabic.

Community

Status Trio has a Chinese-language community for questions, feedback, and release discussion.

  • QQ group: 735856753 — scan the QR code below.
  • WeChat group: scan the QR code below.

  

Privacy

Status Trio reads system status locally. Optional anonymous usage statistics are sent to the first-party service only after you enable them; upgrades start with statistics off, and new installs ask during onboarding. The heartbeat contains a random installation ID, app and macOS versions, language, and icon placement, with no names, account details, network details, or hardware identifiers. See telemetry and privacy. Status Trio does not read or store Wi-Fi passwords or request Keychain access. Location access is optional for the current Wi-Fi network name and details; Bluetooth access is requested when you enable the Bluetooth panel. The optional charge-to-full control uses a private PowerUI interface only when enabled; see known limitations for its behavior and limits.

Development

Run the risk-sized local verification (no GitHub Actions, signing, or release):

bash scripts/verify-local.sh quick BatteryMonitorTests
bash scripts/verify-local.sh docs
bash scripts/verify-local.sh full

Use quick for an isolated code change, docs for documentation or localization-only work, and full for state, concurrency, rendering, Helper, or build-pipeline changes. full builds a non-Universal development app bundle; it does not produce the release package.

When you need only a focused Swift test, keep using the existing test helper:

bash scripts/test.sh BatteryMonitorTests

Formal release verification is separate from daily development. A merged change is not a built artifact, and a built artifact is not a released version.

To build a worktree app alongside the main installation:

bash scripts/build-worktree.sh release

The helper derives a development bundle identifier and display name from the current branch. Both values can be overridden:

BUNDLE_ID=com.lingsmbp.StatusTrio.dev.settings-redesign \
APP_NAME="Status Trio (Settings Redesign)" \
bash scripts/build-worktree.sh release

The single-instance lock is scoped by bundle identifier, so differently identified builds can run at the same time.

Icon presentation API

For the three icon regions, update timing, Swift examples, and extension boundaries, see 三图形展示与更新 API. This documents the current internal API; an external plugin SDK is not implemented.

Technical baseline

  • Swift 6
  • SwiftUI + AppKit
  • macOS 13 deployment target (Ventura runtime validation pending)
  • LSUIElement menu bar accessory that switches to a regular activation policy while the Dock icon is shown
  • Sparkle for update checks

Documentation

  • Known limitations
  • Battery power flow and CPU energy impact
  • Charge to Full Now: behavior and verification
  • Status panel global shortcut
  • Automated GitHub Actions releases
  • Status Trio design specification
  • Menu bar icon SVG
  • Data-driven icon demo

License

Copyright 2026 lingyired.

Status Trio is licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0. See LICENSE and NOTICE.

Bundled third-party components carry their own licenses and do not change the project's Apache-2.0 license:

  • Third-party licenses and dependency notices
  • Third-party source and build/replacement instructions

Author

Created and maintained by lingyired.
Website: https://statustrio.lingai.net/

item.title: manaflow-ai/cmux
item.description:
Open source Ghostty-based macOS terminal with vertical tabs and notifications for AI coding agents. Built for multitasking, organization, and programmability.

https://cmux.com

cmux

A Ghostty-based macOS terminal with vertical tabs and notifications for AI coding agents

English | 日本語 | Tiếng Việt | 简体中文 | 繁體中文 | 한국어 | Deutsch | Español | Français | Italiano | Dansk | Polski | Русский | Bosanski | العربية | Norsk | Português (Brasil) | ไทย | Türkçe | ភាសាខ្មែរ | Українська

▶ Demo video · The Zen of cmux

Docs · Blog · Changelog · Community

Features

Notification rings

Panes get a blue ring and tabs light up when coding agents need your attention

Notification panel

See all pending notifications in one place, jump to the most recent unread

In-app browser

Split a browser alongside your terminal with a scriptable API ported from agent-browser

Vertical + horizontal tabs

Sidebar shows git branch, linked PR status/number, working directory, listening ports, and latest notification text. Split horizontally and vertically.

SSH

cmux ssh user@remote creates a workspace for a remote machine. Pass --command 'omp "investigate auth"' to run an initial command once in its first remote terminal. Browser panes route through the remote network so localhost just works. Drag an image into a remote session to upload via scp.

Claude Code Teams

cmux claude-teams runs Claude Code's teammate mode with one command. Teammates spawn as native splits with sidebar metadata and notifications. No tmux required.
  • Browser import — Import cookies, history, and sessions from Chrome, Firefox, Arc, and 20+ browsers so browser panes start authenticated
  • Custom commands — Define project-specific actions in cmux.json that launch from the command palette
  • Programmable — CLI and socket API to create workspaces, split panes, send keystrokes, and automate the browser
  • Native macOS app — Built with Swift and AppKit, not Electron. Fast startup, low memory.
  • Ghostty compatible — Reads your existing ~/.config/ghostty/config for themes, fonts, and colors
  • GPU-accelerated — Powered by libghostty for smooth rendering
  • Keyboard shortcuts — Extensive shortcuts for workspaces, splits, browser, and more
  • Open source — Free and GPL-licensed

Install

DMG (recommended)

Open the .dmg and drag cmux to your Applications folder. cmux auto-updates via Sparkle, so you only need to download once.

Homebrew

brew tap manaflow-ai/cmux
brew install --cask cmux

To update later:

brew upgrade --cask cmux

On first launch, macOS may ask you to confirm opening an app from an identified developer. Click Open to proceed.

Shell completion

The Homebrew cask installs completions for zsh, bash, and fish. Start a new shell after installing. If they don't load, make sure Homebrew's completion directories are wired into your shell (see Homebrew's shell completion docs).

If you installed cmux another way, add the matching line to your shell startup file, then start a new shell:

autoload -Uz compinit && compinit
eval "$(cmux completion zsh)"

eval "$(cmux completion bash)"

cmux completion fish | source

Why cmux?

I run a lot of Claude Code and Codex sessions in parallel. I was using Ghostty with a bunch of split panes, and relying on native macOS notifications to know when an agent needed me. But Claude Code's notification body is always just "Claude is waiting for your input" with no context, and with enough tabs open I couldn't even read the titles anymore.

I tried a few coding orchestrators but most of them were Electron/Tauri apps and the performance bugged me. I also just prefer the terminal since GUI orchestrators lock you into their workflow. So I built cmux as a native macOS app in Swift/AppKit. It uses libghostty for terminal rendering and reads your existing Ghostty config for themes, fonts, and colors.

The main additions are the sidebar and notification system. The sidebar has vertical tabs that show git branch, linked PR status/number, working directory, listening ports, and the latest notification text for each workspace. The notification system picks up terminal sequences (OSC 9/99/777) and has a CLI (cmux notify) you can wire into agent hooks for Claude Code, OpenCode, etc. When an agent is waiting, its pane gets a blue ring and the tab lights up in the sidebar, so I can tell which one needs me across splits and tabs. Cmd+Shift+U jumps to the most recent unread.

The in-app browser has a scriptable API ported from agent-browser. Agents can snapshot the accessibility tree, get element refs, click, fill forms, and evaluate JS. You can split a browser pane next to your terminal and have Claude Code interact with your dev server directly.

Everything is scriptable through the CLI and socket API — create workspaces/tabs, split panes, send keystrokes, open URLs in the browser.

The Zen of cmux

cmux is not prescriptive about how developers hold their tools. It's a terminal and browser with a CLI, and the rest is up to you.

cmux is a primitive, not a solution. It gives you a terminal, a browser, notifications, workspaces, splits, tabs, and a CLI to control all of it. cmux doesn't force you into an opinionated way to use coding agents. What you build with the primitives is yours.

The best developers have always built their own tools. Nobody has figured out the best way to work with agents yet, and the teams building closed products definitely haven't either. The developers closest to their own codebases will figure it out first.

Give a million developers composable primitives and they'll collectively find the most efficient workflows faster than any product team could design top-down.

Documentation

For more info on how to configure cmux, head over to our docs.

To theme cmux (colors, fonts, transparency, sidebar, and more), see Customizing cmux's look.

For shell watcher churn and managed-Mac process audit volume, see the supported CMUX_NO_GIT_WATCH=1 mitigation and its Git/PR update trade-offs.

Keyboard Shortcuts

Workspaces

Shortcut Action
⌘ N New local workspace
⌘ Y New Cloud workspace on the last usable Cloud context; opens New Cloud Machine when none is available
⌘ ⇧ Y New Cloud machine
⌘ 1–8 Jump to workspace 1–8
⌘ 9 Jump to last workspace
⌃ ⌘ ] Next workspace
⌃ ⌘ [ Previous workspace
⌘ ⇧ W Close workspace
⌘ ⇧ R Rename workspace
⌥ ⌘ E Edit workspace description
⌘ B Toggle sidebar
⌥ ⌘ B Toggle right sidebar
⌘ ⇧ E Toggle right sidebar focus

Surfaces

Shortcut Action
⌘ T New surface
⌘ ⇧ ] Next surface
⌘ ⇧ [ Previous surface
⌃ Tab Next surface
⌃ ⇧ Tab Previous surface
⌃ 1–8 Jump to surface 1–8
⌃ 9 Jump to last surface
⌘ W Close surface

Split Panes

Shortcut Action
⌘ D Split right
⌘ ⇧ D Split down
⌥ ⌘ ← → ↑ ↓ Focus pane directionally
⌃ ⇧ H J K L Resize pane left/down/up/right
⌘ ⇧ H Flash focused panel

Browser

Browser developer-tool shortcuts follow Safari defaults and are customizable in Settings → Keyboard Shortcuts. Command palette navigation shortcuts, including ⌃ P, are also customizable and can be cleared so the keypress reaches the active terminal.

Window
